quizzes.title: Key terms and ideas
quizzes.intro: Ten quick checks on the vocabulary of the accounting equation and Ahmed’s canteen.

questions.q: Accounting is best described as the process of…
options: Buying and selling goods for a profit
Recording, sorting and summarising the data from business transactions
Calculating the tax a business must pay
Fixing the selling price of a product
questions.explain: The lecture defines accounting as recording, sorting and summarising transaction data. Pricing and tax use accounting records but are not accounting itself.

questions.q: Which of the following is a ‘right to property’ rather than property itself?
questions.explain: Creditors have a claim on the assets, so they are a right to property. Cash, equipment and supplies are the property (assets) that the claims are held against.

questions.q: In the accounting equation, the owner’s capital is placed on the same side as the liabilities.
questions.explain: Liabilities + Capital = Assets. Both owners and creditors hold claims on the assets, so capital sits with liabilities on the ‘right to property’ side.

questions.q: A business transaction is defined in the lecture as…
options: Any cash payment made by the owner
An event that transfers goods or renders services and must be recorded
A sale made to a customer on credit
A change in the market value of equipment
questions.explain: A transaction is an event that transfers goods or renders services and must be recorded. A sale on credit is only one example; a change in market value is not recorded at all.

questions.q: Which of these events reduces Ahmed’s capital?
options: Buying supplies on credit for Rs 650
questions.explain: Drawings reduce capital. Sales increase it; buying supplies on credit and paying creditors change assets and liabilities but leave capital untouched.

questions.q: Recording depreciation of equipment reduces both the asset total and the capital.
questions.explain: Depreciation is entered as accumulated depreciation (a deduction from equipment) and as a reduction of capital, so both sides fall by the same amount and the equation still balances.

questions.q: In Ahmed’s worksheet, ‘Accumulated Depreciation’ is best described as…
options: A liability owed to the equipment supplier
A deduction from the equipment asset
An amount of cash set aside for a new machine
questions.explain: Assets = Cash + Supplies + Equipment − Acc. Dep.: accumulated depreciation is subtracted from equipment. No cash is set aside and no one is owed money.

questions.q: How did Ahmed find the supplies used during the month?
options: Supplies bought minus supplies left at month end
Supplies bought plus supplies left at month end
questions.explain: Supplies used = bought (650) − left at month end (250) = 400. Cash paid to creditors (300) tells you nothing about how much was consumed.

questions.q: If the two columns of the trial balance agree, every transaction must have been recorded correctly.
questions.explain: Agreement only shows that each transaction was recorded on both sides. A transaction recorded in the wrong account, or omitted altogether, still leaves the columns equal.

questions.q: When Ahmed buys food supplies on credit, which two items change?
questions.explain: Supplies (an asset) rise by 650 and Trade Creditors (a liability) rise by 650. No cash moves until the creditors are paid in transaction d.

quizzes.title: Formulas and relationships
quizzes.intro: How the equation rearranges and which way each balance moves when a transaction is recorded.

questions.q: Rearranging the accounting equation, the owner’s capital equals…
questions.explain: Since Liabilities + Capital = Assets, Capital = Assets − Liabilities. Adding liabilities to assets double-counts the creditors’ claim.

questions.q: Ahmed buys kitchen equipment for Rs 17,400 cash. What happens to total assets?
questions.explain: One asset (cash) falls and another (equipment) rises by the same amount, so the total is unchanged. Only the mix of assets changes.

questions.q: Paying Rs 300 to creditors has which effect on the equation?
questions.explain: Cash (asset) falls by 300 and Trade Creditors (liability) fall by 300. Capital is not involved because paying a debt is not an expense.

questions.q: At month end Ahmed has cash Rs 2,100, supplies Rs 250, equipment Rs 17,400 and accumulated depreciation Rs 200. What are his total assets?
questions.explain: Assets = 2,100 + 250 + 17,400 − 200 = Rs 19,550. Accumulated depreciation is subtracted, not added.

questions.q: Cash sales increase both the assets and the capital of the business.
questions.explain: Cash (an asset) rises and, because sales are income, capital rises by the same amount — transaction e adds 2,000 to both cash and capital.

questions.q: Which transaction has no effect on capital?
questions.explain: Buying supplies on credit raises an asset and a liability. Wages, depreciation and drawings all reduce capital.

questions.q: Ahmed started with capital Rs 19,000. During the month: sales Rs 2,000, expenses Rs 700, supplies used Rs 400, depreciation Rs 200 and drawings Rs 500. What is his closing capital?
questions.explain: Closing capital = 19,000 + 2,000 − 700 − 400 − 200 − 500 = Rs 19,200. Sales add; every other item subtracts.

questions.q: A depreciation entry of Rs 200 changes the equation by…
questions.explain: Accumulated depreciation reduces the asset side by 200 and the expense reduces capital by 200. The equation must change on both sides or it would no longer balance.

questions.q: If the ‘Liabilities & capital’ column of the trial balance does not equal the ‘Assets’ column, the most likely cause is…
options: A transaction was recorded on one side only
Sales for the month were too low
The owner withdrew too much cash
questions.explain: The lecture states that a disagreement means a transaction was recorded on one side only. Low sales or high drawings are recorded on both sides and keep the columns equal.

questions.q: Drawings are an operating expense of the business.
questions.explain: Drawings reduce capital, but they are the owner taking his own money out, not a cost of running the canteen. They never appear among the expenses in the profit and loss account.

quizzes.title: Worked calculations
quizzes.intro: Work through the balances of Ahmed’s canteen and a second canteen of your own.

questions.q: Equipment cost Rs 17,400 and depreciation of Rs 200 has been charged. What is the net value of the equipment?
questions.explain: Net equipment = 17,400 − 200 = Rs 17,200.

questions.q: Supplies bought during the month cost Rs 650 and supplies worth Rs 250 are left at month end. What is the supplies expense?
questions.explain: Supplies used = 650 − 250 = Rs 400.

questions.q: Ahmed deposits Rs 19,000, pays Rs 17,400 for equipment, pays creditors Rs 300, receives sales Rs 2,000, pays expenses Rs 700 and withdraws Rs 500. What is the closing cash balance?
Supplies of Rs 650 were bought on credit and Rs 300 was later paid to the supplier. What balance is owed to creditors?
questions.explain: Creditors = 650 − 300 = Rs 350.

questions.q: Sara opens a canteen with Rs 50,000 capital. In the first month: cash sales Rs 9,000; cash expenses Rs 2,800; supplies used Rs 2,600; depreciation Rs 500; drawings Rs 1,000. What is her closing capital?
Sara starts with Rs 50,000 cash, buys equipment for Rs 30,000 cash, pays creditors Rs 1,500, receives cash sales Rs 9,000, pays expenses Rs 2,800 and withdraws Rs 1,000. What is her cash balance?
Sara has cash Rs 23,700, bought supplies of Rs 4,000 of which Rs 2,600 were used, equipment Rs 30,000 and accumulated depreciation Rs 500. What are her total assets?
Transaction f lists wages 550, rent 50, utilities 25 and misc 75. The total cash paid is…
questions.explain: 550 + 50 + 25 + 75 = Rs 700. Rs 650 leaves out the rent; Rs 725 adds the utilities twice.

questions.q: Sales were Rs 2,000; wages Rs 550, rent Rs 50, utilities Rs 25, misc Rs 75, supplies used Rs 400 and depreciation Rs 200. What is the profit for the month?
Total assets are Rs 19,550 and capital is Rs 19,200. Liabilities must be…
questions.explain: Liabilities = Assets − Capital = 19,550 − 19,200 = Rs 350. Adding the two figures (38,750) is a reversed formula.

quizzes.title: Applied in practice
quizzes.intro: Take the canteen logic into a textile mill: how everyday events are recorded and what goes wrong when they are not.

questions.q: A weaving mill buys yarn worth Rs 800,000 on 30 days’ credit. What is the immediate effect on its records?
questions.explain: Nothing is paid yet, so an asset (yarn stock) and a liability (creditors) both rise — exactly like Ahmed’s supplies bought on credit.

questions.q: The mill owner takes Rs 20,000 from the cash till for household expenses. How should the accountant record it?
options: As a loan to a creditor
questions.explain: Money taken by the owner is drawings. Recording it as wages would understate profit; it is not a business expense.

questions.q: An accountant records a machine purchase by reducing cash but forgets to add the machine to equipment. What will the trial balance show?
options: The assets column is short by the machine’s cost
The liabilities column is short by the machine’s cost
questions.explain: The transaction was recorded on one side only (cash down, equipment not up), so the assets column is smaller than liabilities plus capital. The trial balance catches this.

questions.q: A loom bought for Rs 1,500,000 should be written off as an expense of the month in which it is bought.
questions.explain: The loom is equipment — an asset with a long life. Only its depreciation becomes an expense each period, as with Ahmed’s Rs 200 on kitchen equipment.

questions.q: Why does a costing course for textile engineers begin with financial accounting?
options: Because engineers must prepare the company’s tax return
Because costs are built from records of money, property and obligations that the engineer must be able to read
Because accounting is easier than costing
questions.explain: The lecture’s argument: before costing a yarn or fabric you must be able to read the records in which money, property and obligations are written — and those records rest on the accounting equation.

questions.q: A spinning mill charges annual depreciation on its ring frames. Which balances change?
questions.explain: Depreciation is a non-cash entry: accumulated depreciation rises (reducing net equipment) and capital falls by the expense. No cash leaves the business.

questions.q: Which of the following is an asset of Ahmed’s canteen at month end?
questions.explain: Unused supplies are property that will give benefit next month. Creditors are a liability, and wages and drawings are reductions of capital.

questions.q: A mill has cash Rs 150,000, yarn stock Rs 320,000, machines costing Rs 2,400,000 with accumulated depreciation Rs 600,000, trade creditors Rs 410,000 and a bank loan Rs 900,000. What is the owners’ capital?
Supplies of Rs 650 were bought and Rs 250 remain, but the accountant charges the full Rs 650 as expense. What is the result?
options: Profit is understated by Rs 250 and the supplies asset is missing
The trial balance will not agree
questions.explain: Only 400 was used. Charging 650 understates profit by 250 and leaves out the 250 of supplies still on the shelf. Both sides fall equally, so the trial balance still agrees.

questions.q: The trial balance is prepared from the month-end balances of the accounts, not by listing every single transaction.
questions.explain: At month end the balances (cash 2,100, supplies 250 and so on) are listed with assets on one side and rights to property on the other. Individual transactions stay in the worksheet or journal.

quizzes.title: Challenge review
quizzes.intro: Harder questions that combine two steps or expose a common mistake.

questions.q: If Ahmed charges Rs 200 depreciation each month, at what net value will the equipment (cost Rs 17,400) appear after two months?
questions.explain: Accumulated depreciation after two months = 2 × 200 = 400, so net equipment = 17,400 − 400 = Rs 17,000. Rs 17,200 is the value after only one month.

questions.q: Ahmed’s closing capital is Rs 19,200. Next month he repeats transactions e to i exactly: sales Rs 2,000, cash expenses Rs 700, supplies used Rs 400, depreciation Rs 200 and drawings Rs 500. What is capital at the end of the second month?
questions.explain: Capital = 19,200 + 2,000 − 700 − 400 − 200 − 500 = Rs 19,400. The month adds a net Rs 200 (profit 700 less drawings 500).

questions.q: Which of Ahmed’s transactions changes the asset side only, leaving liabilities and capital untouched?
questions.explain: Buying equipment for cash swaps one asset for another. Depositing capital and depreciation change capital; buying on credit changes creditors.

questions.q: A student treats Rs 500 of drawings as an expense. What is the effect on the reported figures?
options: Profit is overstated and capital overstated
Profit is understated but closing capital is correct
Profit is correct but capital is understated
The trial balance will not agree
questions.explain: Both drawings and expenses reduce capital, so closing capital comes out right; but profit is understated by 500 because drawings are not a cost of trading.

questions.q: Paying a creditor reduces the capital of the business.
questions.explain: Paying a creditor settles a liability with an asset: cash and creditors both fall. Capital changes only through income, expenses, contributions and drawings.

questions.q: Ahmed’s closing capital was Rs 19,200 with sales of Rs 2,000. If every other figure stayed the same but sales had been Rs 3,500, what would closing capital have been?
questions.explain: Extra sales = 3,500 − 2,000 = 1,500, all of which flows into capital: 19,200 + 1,500 = Rs 20,700.

questions.q: In the basic-form trial balance, how do the expense accounts and drawings fit into the ‘Liabilities & capital’ column that totals Rs 19,550?
options: They are added, because they are claims on the business
They are deducted, because they reduce capital
They are moved to the assets column
questions.explain: Capital 19,000 + creditors 350 + sales 2,000 = 21,350; less expenses 1,300 and drawings 500 = 19,550. Expenses and drawings are deductions from capital on that side.

questions.q: Supplies of Rs 650 are bought on credit, Rs 300 is paid to the supplier, and then a further Rs 200 of supplies is bought on credit. What is now owed to creditors?
Which of the following would NOT be recorded as a business transaction of the canteen this month?
options: Ahmed agrees verbally to buy a refrigerator next month
A customer pays cash for lunch
Ahmed takes Rs 500 for personal use
questions.explain: No goods or services have yet been transferred, so a promise to buy next month is not a transaction. The other three transfer cash or services and must be recorded.

questions.q: If Ahmed’s drawings had been Rs 700 instead of Rs 500, the net profit for the month would fall by Rs 200.
questions.explain: Drawings are not an expense, so profit stays at 700. Closing capital would fall by 200, from 19,200 to 19,000.
